clue.text: Repeated rhythm: how to make par (and golf as well as pals!)

definitions.meaning: a steady pulse that recurs through a piece of music, especially the accented off-beat

definitions.text: how to make par (and golf as well as pals!)
definitions.meaning: read as an instruction, 'back' a 'beat': rap, flog and slap all mean hit, and turned around they read par, golf and pals

explanation.surface: A puzzling golf tip about making par, with friends tagging along, attached to a musical definition.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a pun: to back (turn round) a beat. RAP, FLOG and SLAP all mean beat, and read backwards each gives one of the bracketed words.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: the term musicians use for the regular stressed pulse behind a song, repeated bar after bar.

clue.text: Flashy stuff British swimmer's cloned

indicators.note: a clone is an exact copy, so the piece built here appears twice

parts.note: a ling is a long sea fish, a crossword 'swimmer'

explanation.surface: A British swimmer showing off showy gear that has been copied.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swimmer' is a crossword favourite for a fish; here the ling.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang synonym: showy jewellery and ostentatious accessories are called by this doubled word.

clue.text: Salt originally added to fish with batter on for cobblers

parts.note: the cod is a familiar food fish

indicators.note: originally points to the opening letter of the word salt

parts.note: to batter is to wallop, hit hard

explanation.surface: A fish-and-chip shop recipe: salted fish with batter on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Batter' looks culinary but is the verb hit. 'Cobblers' is British slang for nonsense, not shoemakers.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are British slang words for rubbish or nonsense talk.

clue.text: Something fired up under black crow

indicators.note: in a down answer the second piece sits under the first, so it comes after it

parts.note: B is the pencil-lead abbreviation for black
an oast is a kiln for drying hops, which is heated by a fire

explanation.surface: A black crow perched below something set alight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crow' is not the bird but the verb to brag.
explanation.definitionFit: To crow is to brag loudly about one's own success, so the verb senses match.

clue.text: Chemical expert sits on the deadly liquid

indicators.note: in a down answer the first piece sits on top of the second

parts.note: an ace is an expert

indicators.note: liquid suggests something fluid, so these letters flow into a new order

explanation.surface: A chemistry expert guarding a deadly fluid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'liquid' rearranges THE DEADLY into TALDEHYDE.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a specific organic compound, an aldehyde produced when the body breaks down alcohol.

clue.text: Cold-shoulders wallies

parts.note: C is the tap abbreviation for cold
to shoulder a load is to hump it, carry it

explanation.surface: Fools being snubbed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cold-shoulders' looks like one verb meaning snubs; split it. Wally is British slang for an idiot.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms: both are informal British words for foolish, stupid people.

clue.text: Both sides of having girl — that makes things clearer!

parts.note: the two outer letters of having are H and G, written out with the word between them
lass is a word for a girl

explanation.surface: Someone with a girl on each side, in a way that clarifies matters.
explanation.walkthrough: The joining word between the two end letters is spelt out in full, so 'Both sides of having' gives H, AND, G.
explanation.definitionFit: Descriptive: a small magnifying lens held in the hand enlarges fine print so it can be seen more plainly.

clue.text: 60s' person who's scared — I knew you'd say that!

parts.note: sixty seconds make a minute, abbreviated min
someone who dreads things is a dreader

explanation.surface: A frightened person from the 1960s, met with a knowing exclamation.
explanation.walkthrough: '60s' looks like the decade but is sixty seconds.
explanation.definitionFit: Exemplifying: a telepath would claim to know what you were going to say before you said it.

clue.text: Regularly sees main match before final

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter of sees main, starting with the first

explanation.surface: Someone watching the main game ahead of the final.
explanation.definitionFit: The round of games played just before the deciding one in a knockout tournament.

clue.text: Headwind I am enduring to harbour ships

indicators.note: to harbour is to hold within, so the letters lie inside Headwind I am enduring

explanation.surface: Ships heading into wind as they make for harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'harbour' looks nautical but is the verb to hold inside.
explanation.definitionFit: These were large merchant vessels trading with India for the East India Company.

clue.text: Fictitious name soon to get Screw's backing

parts.note: anon is an old word for soon

indicators.note: backing means the word given by Screw's is read backwards

parts.note: Screw is the setter, so the setter's is my

explanation.surface: A pseudonym about to get the setter's support.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often refer to themselves by name; Screw's means 'my'.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a pen name or assumed name used in place of one's real name.

clue.text: Main distance from actual line I'm dancing

indicators.note: dancing has the letters of actual line I'm moving about into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone dancing a long way from the real line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' is the poetic word for the sea, not 'chief'.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit of length used at sea, so it is literally a measure of distance on the main.

clue.text: Suit, black with silver border, to be carried off brilliantly

parts.note: to go with something is to suit it, match it

indicators.note: silver bordering black means its letters sit either side of the other piece

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
to black something is to boycott or ban it, in trade-union usage

explanation.surface: Describing a fine outfit: a black suit trimmed with silver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'black' is the verb to boycott, giving BAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: an event that succeeds spectacularly is said to end with a flourish like an explosion.

clue.text: Change a result — it'd sound like cricket?

indicators.note: change tells us to alter the order of the letters in a result it'd

explanation.surface: Altering the result of a cricket match, it would seem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cricket' is the chirping insect, not the game.
explanation.definitionFit: Grasshoppers and crickets make their chirping noise by rubbing body parts together, which this verb names.

clue.text: Having three sides after filling in test

indicators.note: filling in says one word fills the middle of another

parts.note: a trial is a test
later means after

explanation.surface: Completing a test form, with a remark about three sides.
explanation.definitionFit: Geometric description: a figure with tri- (three) lateral (side) edges, like a triangle.

clue.text: I call mobile, getting tone

indicators.note: mobile means able to move, so the letters of I call move about

explanation.surface: Making a mobile phone call and hearing a dial tone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tone' suggests a ring tone; it is a colour shade.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a pale purple shade named after a flowering shrub.

clue.text: Battle between black and white bags Lidl supply without issue

indicators.note: bags means seizes or holds, so one piece is held inside the other

parts.note: chess is a contest between the black and white pieces

indicators.note: supply is read as an adverb, supplely, so the letters of Lidl bend into a new order

explanation.surface: A fight at the supermarket over shopping bags. Lidl is a budget supermarket chain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supply' is not the noun but 'in a supple way'; it rearranges LIDL into ILDL.
explanation.definitionFit: Issue in the legal sense means offspring, so having none means no children.

clue.text: One critical of French farmer's tower

parts.note: de is the French word for of
a tractor tows things for a farmer, so it is a 'tower'

explanation.surface: A critic of a French farmer's tower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tower' is one who tows, not a tall building.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: someone who disparages or belittles another is a critic of them.

clue.text: Break into Chile, just like the old days?

indicators.note: break means to smash the letters of into Chile and reassemble them

explanation.surface: Breaking into Chile, as people might have in earlier times.
explanation.definitionFit: It describes the late Stone Age, so it belongs to the very old days; the question mark flags the understatement.

clue.text: Smooth, even now

definitions.meaning: to smooth or calm troubled waters, quieten them
as an adverb meaning up to this moment, continuing

explanation.surface: A short description of calm, unchanging conditions.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a verb meaning to calm, and an adverb meaning yet or up to now.

clue.text: FA team in pub, possibly swapping tips!

indicators.note: swapping tips means the first and last letters of the phrase change places

parts.note: someone in a pub might be tiddly, slightly drunk
a squad is a team

explanation.surface: A Football Association team at the pub, exchanging advice.
explanation.walkthrough: FA is not the Football Association but 'Fanny Adams', British slang for nothing at all. TIDDLY SQUAD with its end letters T and D exchanged.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are British slang for absolutely nothing; sweet FA is a euphemism of the same kind.

clue.text: Pilot Officer cuts short easy takeoff

indicators.note: cuts means one piece slices into the middle of another
short means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: soft means easy, as in a soft option
PO is the RAF abbreviation for Pilot Officer

explanation.surface: An RAF pilot making a gentle takeoff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takeoff' is not an aircraft leaving the ground but a parody. 'short' trims SOFT to SOF.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a takeoff of someone is an imitation or parody, a light-hearted send-up.

clue.text: Timeless body … ish!

indicators.note: read as time-less, it says to drop T, the abbreviation for time

parts.note: the torso is the trunk of the body

explanation.surface: A body that never ages, roughly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Timeless' looks like ageless but splits into time (T) less.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are used after a figure to mean approximately, more or less.

clue.text: Did utter sod ask it during openings?

indicators.note: openings means the first letters of sod ask it during

explanation.surface: Did someone curse while asking a question at the openings?
explanation.definitionFit: Past tense of a speaking verb: to have uttered words is to have spoken them.

clue.text: See 7
Unimportant that Greek character cuts monster

indicators.note: cuts means one piece slices into the middle of another

parts.note: minor means unimportant
tau is a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: A minor Greek character in a story sliced into a monster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'character' is a letter, not a person in a story.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the bull-headed creature of Greek myth kept in the Cretan labyrinth.

clue.text: Who'd destroy housing out there more than others?

indicators.note: housing means holding within, so the letters lie inside Who'd destroy

explanation.surface: Asking who would demolish houses in some remote place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out there' is slang for weird or unconventional, here in superlative form.
explanation.definitionFit: Being 'out there' means being strange, so being more so than anyone else is the superlative of strange.

clue.text: An option as he fell ill?

definitions.text: An option as he fell ill?

indicators.note: ill means in a bad state, so the letters of as he fell are reworked

explanation.surface: Someone taken ill wondering whether he could cure himself.
explanation.walkthrough: It is also a wild plant, prunella, once used to treat wounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Curing oneself is one possible course when unwell; the herb's name also says it heals.
